title: Why the UK, Spain and the EU agreed a bespoke deal for Gibraltar
label: 15 September 2026 · UK‑EU Agreement on Gibraltar
summary: Ministers from the Foreign Office explained why Gibraltar was left out of the 2020 UK‑EU Trade and Co‑operation Agreement, what the new bespoke treaty does, how it protects Gibraltar’s open land border, and why the UK says sovereignty isn’t affected. Committee members pushed on issues such as the role of Spanish officials, policing, military access, legal checks by EU courts, exit clauses and costs. Ministers said the deal replaces informal measures with a legally backed system designed to keep the border fluid while preserving UK control of Gibraltar.

chapters.title: Why Gibraltar needed its own deal
chapters.takeaway: Gibraltar wasn’t in the 2020 UK‑EU deal so the governments agreed a separate, tailor‑made treaty to secure an open land border and legal certainty.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why wasn’t Gibraltar included in the 2020 UK‑EU Trade and Co‑operation Agreement, and why did it take five years to get a separate deal?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Gibraltar was left out of the 2020 deal because the EU treated it differently, partly because Spain wanted separate arrangements. The result was uncertainty for people and business in Gibraltar, so the UK, Gibraltar, Spain and the EU later negotiated a bespoke treaty to secure the open land border and give long‑term certainty.

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: It took a long time because the treaty is complex—many chapters, technical issues (airport checks, customs, military matters) and new physical and IT arrangements had to be built. Politics in the UK and Spain over the last five years also slowed progress.

turns.speaker: Baroness Suttie
turns.text: What problem from Brexit was this treaty mainly trying to fix?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The big Brexit risk was the return of full immigration checks at the land border. That would have been disastrous for Gibraltar and cross‑border workers. The treaty replaces informal 'bridging measures'—agreements based on goodwill—with a lasting legal framework.

chapters.title: What the agreement actually does
chapters.takeaway: The deal keeps the land border 'fluid' by letting people cross without routine checks, sets customs rules for goods, and creates joint bodies to manage the arrangements.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: You use the phrase 'fluidity at the frontier'—what does that mean in practice versus full free movement?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: It means roughly 15,000 people a day can cross the Gibraltar‑Spain land border without routine checks. Air and sea travel have different checks. The priority was avoiding daily disruption that would harm jobs and the local economy.

turns.speaker: Lord Grantchester
turns.text: Who manages this complicated arrangement day to day? Will the UK need more diplomats?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The treaty creates joint governance bodies: a ministerial co‑operation council, specialized committees and dispute procedures. The UK already has teams in Whitehall, Brussels and Madrid plus the Governor in Gibraltar. We don’t expect a big boost in resources; it’s more about steady engagement.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: On trade: the agreement covers goods. Gibraltar has opted for a bespoke customs arrangement with the EU for goods but pursues services trade internationally itself.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: So Gibraltar can sign trade deals on services—like joining CPTPP—but not for goods because of this customs arrangement?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: Yes. Goods are covered by the customs arrangement with the EU; services remain Gibraltar’s area and it could, in principle, join international service agreements.

chapters.title: Sovereignty concerns and Spanish cooperation
chapters.takeaway: The Government says sovereignty isn’t affected: Gibraltar chose many of the arrangements, but Spanish officials will have limited roles (e.g., Schengen checks) which some worry could grow over time.

turns.speaker: Baroness Ashton of Upholland
turns.text: Does any part of the treaty challenge UK sovereignty over Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: No. Article 2 of the treaty explicitly says the agreement doesn’t affect the sovereignty position. Sovereignty wasn’t negotiated away. The treaty covers technical, operational arrangements that Gibraltar agreed to.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: But if Gibraltar is in a customs union‑style arrangement for goods with the EU, isn’t that an impingement on UK trade policy?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Gibraltar chose a bespoke customs arrangement for goods with the EU. That’s not the UK joining the EU customs union; it’s a specific solution for Gibraltar to secure the border and its economy.

turns.speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough
turns.text: The treaty lists lots of powers for Spain and the EU—arrests, visa blocking and permit reviews. Doesn’t that undermine British sovereignty?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The list isn’t what it seems. Many annexes are procedural or lists of offences; only a small number refer to EU law. Crucially, Gibraltar opted into certain rules to get the benefits of an open border. That’s a choice by Gibraltar, not a transfer of UK sovereignty.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: Is there a risk of a 'creeping' expansion of Spanish authority inside Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The treaty defines limited, clearly framed roles for Spanish authorities—for example Spanish officials do Schengen checks at Gibraltar airport. Military and law enforcement roles are tightly delimited. Gibraltar and the UK keep control of core functions.

chapters.title: Checks, policing, courts and the dispute process
chapters.takeaway: Spanish officials will do some Schengen checks; Gibraltar keeps final say on entry. The EU court can be asked to interpret EU law parts, and the treaty has dispute and referral procedures similar to earlier EU deals.

turns.speaker: Baroness Smith of Newnham
turns.text: You said service personnel and families don’t face routine Schengen checks—how will that work with the 90‑days‑in‑180 limit in Schengen countries?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: They’ll use documents like movement orders or ID to show they qualify for a derogation. There’s an arrangement so military time in Gibraltar doesn’t count against the Schengen 90‑days rule—a practical 'clock‑stop/clock‑start'.

turns.speaker: Lord Brennan of Canton
turns.text: Who can refuse entry to someone arriving? Can Spanish authorities effectively bar people from entering Gibraltar?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Gibraltar remains responsible for who it admits. Spain decides entry to the Schengen area. Where Spain refuses someone on security grounds via Schengen systems, Gibraltar has agreed to mutually recognise those decisions for its own entry choices—but Gibraltar keeps the final decision on admitting people to Gibraltar.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: Everyone passing through Gibraltar airport goes through Gibraltar immigration checks and then Schengen checks by Spanish officers. The systems are linked; both checks happen.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: What about the courts? Can the European Court of Justice (the EU’s top court) be involved?

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: The treaty uses a standard arbitration route. For questions that hinge on EU law texts Gibraltar has aligned to, the EU court can be asked to interpret EU law. That’s a precedented mechanism taken from the Withdrawal Agreement and other EU deals.

chapters.title: Exit clauses, costs and next steps
chapters.takeaway: There are several exit routes: a long process requiring Gibraltar consent, a 90‑day route if Gibraltar refuses alignment, and a limited Spanish trigger at a later review; the concordat that sits alongside the treaty is political, not a legal instrument.

turns.speaker: Lord Elliott of Mickle Fell
turns.text: How will the financial mechanism work and who pays?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Both sides will set up funds to help Gibraltar and the neighbouring region—for example training for cross‑border workers. The UK’s contribution is expected to come from Gibraltar’s own resources rather than UK taxpayer funds, under the concordat arrangements.

turns.speaker: Lord Barrow
turns.text: Why was a concordat—an accompanying political agreement—needed, and what legal weight does it have?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: The concordat clarifies how the UK and Gibraltar will implement the treaty in practice. It’s political, not legally binding, and it sets out responsibilities and a way of working so the treaty can function smoothly.

turns.speaker: Lord Moynihan of Chelsea
turns.text: What about termination? I understand Article 334 requires long notice and Gibraltar consent, but there’s also a 90‑day exit and a Spanish trigger—is that correct?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Article 334 is the long route. Article 19.5 is a precedented 90‑day mechanism used in other Schengen‑type deals if Gibraltar explicitly refuses to accept an update it has agreed to. There’s also a Spanish channel linked to a review of mobility at the four‑year mark—that’s not 'any time' but part of a specific review process.

turns.speaker: Paul Hughes
turns.text: To be precise: the Spanish option relates to a mobility review after four years; Spain can ask the EU to trigger a termination process if it’s not content, and that starts a further process. We’ll confirm the exact timing and triggers in writing for clarity.

turns.speaker: Lord Tugendhat
turns.text: Does this settle Gibraltar’s Brexit legacy, or will further talks be needed?

turns.speaker: Lord Wood of Anfield
turns.text: Treaty-wise, this is the last big piece after Brexit. It creates a stable, long‑term framework. There will be practical implementation work and possible adjustments, but the fundamentals are now in place.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Please follow up on the points you’ll confirm in writing (such as entry rules for non‑Spanish EU nationals and the exact wording and timing of the termination provisions). We’ll also hear from the Gibraltar Chief Minister next.

glossary.definition: The 2020 post‑Brexit treaty setting the rules for trade and co‑operation between the United Kingdom and the European Union.
A custom, one‑off international agreement written to deal with specific issues for particular parties.
Temporary, informal steps taken by authorities to keep things working until a formal legal agreement is in place.
The practical ability for people to cross the land border smoothly each day without routine immigration checks.
A formal body where government ministers from the parties meet to oversee and coordinate how a treaty runs.
A shorthand name for the UK central government departments and civil service based in London.
The UK’s official representative in Gibraltar who performs certain constitutional and ceremonial roles on behalf of the Crown.
A tailor‑made set of rules about how goods move across borders, agreed specifically between Gibraltar and the EU.
The Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans‑Pacific Partnership, a large multilateral trade pact among Pacific‑region countries.
A specific numbered clause in the treaty; here it is the clause stating the agreement does not affect sovereignty.
An arrangement where members apply common external tariffs and eliminate customs checks between them, like a customs union.
Supplementary documents attached to a treaty that list detailed rules, procedures or offences.
Border control checks carried out under the Schengen system when someone is entering the Schengen area.
A group of European countries that largely abolished routine passport checks at their internal borders.
The Schengen rule that allows non‑residents to stay a maximum of 90 days in any rolling 180‑day period for short visits.
Official military documents authorising personnel movement and often granting specific travel exemptions.

glossary.term: European Court of Justice (the EU’s top court)
glossary.definition: The highest court interpreting EU law and resolving legal disputes about EU rules.
A dispute‑resolution process where independent arbitrators, not national courts, decide a disagreement under a treaty.
The treaty that set the terms of the UK’s departure from the EU (the main Brexit implementation deal).
A political, non‑legally binding agreement that sets out practical working arrangements between parties.
A specific treaty clause referenced here that establishes a long‑notice route for terminating the agreement.
A specific treaty clause referenced here that provides a precedented 90‑day exit mechanism in certain circumstances.
A formal assessment, scheduled here after four years, to review how cross‑border movement arrangements are working.
The elected head of government of Gibraltar.
Periodic checks to reassess whether issued visas, entry permits or work permits should remain valid.
